title: What happened to BP Spacer? (English rebuild reference)
summary: A 105s vertical explainer (original, rebuilt in English) telling the history of a nostalgic Pakistani toffee brand. Flat, warm-paper 2D illustration with one recurring hero object (the toffee, drawn as a rocket) that travels through every scene, so the whole video feels like one continuous camera move rather than cuts. Structure: nostalgic hook, the question ('why is it rarely seen today?'), origin story via a time dial (1947 Karachi bakery), growth, competition (1988 onward), decline in shops, a twist (still sold in 2013), and an open ending. It works because every abstract idea becomes a visual metaphor (popularity = launch + fireworks, competition = rocket race, product range = constellation, new brands = flags on a moon).

sections.label: Hook
sections.purpose: Nostalgia: the toffee fills a shop jar, kids on a rooftop cheer as it launches like a rocket ('hugely popular').

sections.label: Question
sections.purpose: Today: a telescope searches a modern shop shelf and finds an empty slot. 'Why is it rarely seen now?'

sections.label: Origin
sections.purpose: Time dial spins 2026 to 1951/1947; globe zooms to Karachi; founder on Lawrence Road opens a small bakery: bread, biscuits, cake, then toffees.

sections.label: Rise
sections.purpose: Toffee launches from the bakery dome, bakery grows into BP Industries; product constellation (BP Spacer, Whale Jelly, Chicken Candy).

sections.label: Competition
sections.purpose: 1986-1988: CandyLand plants a flag on the moon, more company flags follow; candies orbit the moon; a child surrounded by options; rocket race on new packaging, ads and shop availability; the toffee falls behind.

sections.label: Twist
sections.purpose: BP never only made toffees (chewing gum, bubble gum, jelly, chocolate, biscuits); old popularity recalled; the toffee orbits the globe; 'not finished': a 2013 news clipping shows it still sells at Rs. 2.

sections.label: Close
sections.purpose: Toffee orbiting softly, dial moves 2013 to 2026; father and child at a telescope at night: it is not gone, just 'out of sight'.

narration.script: You must have eaten plenty of BP Spacer toffees in your childhood too. But do you know why this toffee, once hugely popular with kids, is so rarely seen in the market today? The story begins in Karachi, after Pakistan's independence, when Sheikh Muhammad Yahya started a small bakery business on Nishtar Road. At first he made bread, biscuits and cakes. But later he started making toffees too. And so the journey of BP Industries moved forward, and its famous products came to include sweets like BP Spacer, Whale Jelly and Chicken Candy. But over time, the market began to change. In 1988, Candyland also stepped into the industry. And then new companies began introducing different flavours, jellies and chewing gum. Kids now had far more options than ever before. Meanwhile, competition in the market was growing, where new packaging, advertising and a better presence in shops were becoming more and more important. BP, too, instead of staying limited to toffees, began making chewing gum, bubble gum, jelly, chocolate and biscuits. But despite all this, BP Spacer couldn't hold on to its old popularity. Interestingly, it never disappeared completely. In fact, according to a 2013 report, it was still being sold. So this famous childhood toffee never really ended, but over time it slowly slipped out of sight for a new generation.
